channel.title: Hardwares on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Hardwares on Best of AI

item.title: d-Matrix Raptor
item.description: d-Matrix presented Raptor at Hot Chips 2026, which it calls the first 3D-DRAM accelerator built for generative inference. Rather than routing through a conventional memory PHY, Raptor bonds a TSMC 4nm compute die face-to-face onto a custom-designed DRAM die at a 36-micron pitch, delivering 100 TB/s of bandwidth from 32GB of memory per card at roughly 0.37 picojoules per bit, well below the energy cost of moving data into an HBM4 base die. d-Matrix’s accompanying ISCA 2026 paper projects about 4.7 times higher inference throughput per card than HBM-based designs. The company’s CEO has said Raptor is on track to launch in 2027.

item.title: Intel Crescent Island
item.description: Intel gave a deep technical rundown of its Crescent Island inference GPU at Hot Chips 2026 in August, following up its earlier disclosure of the chip. It packs 32 Xe3P cores, 256 XMX matrix engines, and 32MB of unified L2 cache, and leans on capacity-dense LPDDR5X rather than HBM: the standard air-cooled card ships with 160GB at 350W, with ODM designs supporting up to 480GB for customers who need to fit larger models without a memory-bandwidth-first design. Intel is targeting AI inference and agentic workloads specifically, trading some raw throughput for lower power and higher memory capacity per card. Customer sampling is expected in the second half of 2026, with a full launch slated for 2027.

item.title: Microsoft Maia 200
item.description: Microsoft unveiled Maia 200 in January 2026 as the successor to its first in-house Maia 100 chip, moving from TSMC’s 5nm node to 3nm and packing 144 billion transistors. It carries 216GB of HBM3e memory at 7 TB/s of bandwidth plus 272MB of on-chip SRAM, and delivers around 10 petaflops of FP4 and 5 petaflops of FP8 compute within a 750W envelope, with native FP8/FP4 tensor cores tuned for inference rather than training. Microsoft says it offers roughly 30 percent better performance per dollar than the prior generation. At Hot Chips 2026 in August, Microsoft gave its deepest public look yet at the chip’s architecture as it prepares to deploy Maia 200 across Azure data centers.

item.title: Cerebras CS-4
item.description: Cerebras unveiled the CS-4 on August 18, 2026, built around its new Nexus rack architecture that houses three WSE-3T wafers per system instead of the single wafer used in the CS-3. Each wafer carries 900,000 AI cores and 44GB of on-wafer SRAM, and Cerebras claims up to 30x more tokens-per-second-per-user than GPU-based inference. The modular backpack design roughly doubles power and cooling headroom over the CS-3, and the company has already outlined CS-5 and CS-6 as the next steps on the same platform.

item.title: Meta MTIA 300
item.description: Meta detailed the MTIA 300 on August 24, 2026, its first MTIA chip aimed at large training workloads rather than just inference. It pairs a 12x6 grid of processing elements with 216GB of HBM3E and two network chiplets carrying twelve custom 800 Gbps RDMA NICs, giving each chip 1.2 TB/s of I/O bandwidth so training jobs can scale across racks without relying on separate networking hardware.

item.title: Meta MTIA 400
item.description: Meta detailed the MTIA 400 at Hot Chips 2026, built on a 3nm process with 288GB of HBM3E and a 1200W TDP. Unlike earlier MTIA chips split into separate training and inference lines, the 400 is built to run both jobs on the same silicon, reaching about 12 petaflops of MXFP4 compute and 6 petaflops at FP8. Meta says it plans to ship a new MTIA generation roughly every six months going forward.

item.title: NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX
item.description: Groq 3 LPX is the first chip to ship from Nvidia’s $20 billion acquisition of Groq, announced in production at Hot Chips 2026. Each LP30 die carries around 500MB of on-chip SRAM with 150 TB/s of bandwidth and handles only token generation, not training or prefill. Nvidia pairs the chips into liquid-cooled racks of 256 LPUs as a companion to its Vera Rubin platform, aimed at the low-latency demands of agentic AI workloads.
